fixes.explanation: I get it, it's a river, so water feels like the obvious pick. Good river instinct, friend! But the LORD asks for something else: twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan (Joshua 4:3). Joshua tells each man to take a stone upon his shoulder (Joshua 4:5). Nobody's hauling jars on this trip, just stones.

Visiting traders! Friend, I love the thinking. A stranger rolls into camp, sees twelve big stones piled up, and has questions. But Joshua doesn't mention a single trader. He says the ones asking will be "your children" (Joshua 4:6). The stones are a sign among the Israelites themselves. So the question comes from inside the family, probably right at the dinner table.

Boundary! I see you, friend, a stone marking a line is a real thing. But Joshua doesn't say a word about lines. He calls these stones a memorial to the Israelites forever (Joshua 4:7). They're tied to the waters of the Jordan being cut off before the ark. These stones aren't there to say where something ends. They're there to say what happened.

He exalts him. "On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel…" (Joshua 4:14). The text adds that they revered him all the days of his life, just as they had revered Moses. I think that's quite a day for Joshua. The whole nation watching, and the LORD lifting him up right in front of them. Nobody had to puff him up, friend.
